1.title: What Is Light?
1.text:
What Is Light?

Light is electromagnetic radiation that can be modeled as a wave of changing electric and magnetic fields or as particles called photons.

Our big question for this lesson: how does distance affect how bright a star appears? Let's chase some light!

Light is electromagnetic radiation, like radio waves and microwaves. We can model it as a wave of changing electric and magnetic fields, or as particles called photons. The wave model explains many features of light, and the particle model explains others. In this module, we'll focus on light's wave properties. Photons come later.

How does your body take in information? Sight depends on light from your surroundings reaching your eyes. Think of a flashlight beam or sunlight streaming through a small window, lit up by dust in the air. The path looks like a straight line. And when your body blocks sunlight, you cast a shadow, thanks to that straight path. Figure 1 shows light traveling in straight lines.

2.title: Your Investigation Toolkit
2.text:
Your Investigation Toolkit

Collect evidence in your Science Journal and investigate with activities.

Use your Science Journal to record the evidence you collect as you complete the readings and activities in this lesson.

Online, the Quick Investigation called The Speed of Light uses the relationship among frequency, wavelength, and wave speed to calculate the speed of light. In the Probeware Lab called Light Intensity and Distance, you'll analyze data to find how distance from a source affects the intensity of light.

3.title: The Ray Model of Light
3.text:
The Ray Model of Light

The ray model of light says light travels in straight lines, and its direction can change when it meets a boundary.

Imagine an empty, dark room with a small lightbulb switched on in the middle. You can see all around the room, and you can see the bulb too. So the bulb must send light in all directions. Picture countless arrows streaming straight out of it. Each arrow is a ray of light, and it travels straight until it reaches a boundary, as in Figure 2.

At a boundary, the light can be reflected or refracted. Its direction changes, but it keeps going in a straight line. Those two ideas, that light travels in straight lines and that a boundary can change its direction, make up the ray model of light. Studying how light interacts with matter this way is called ray optics, or geometric optics.

4.title: Luminous and Illuminated Sources
4.text:
Luminous and Illuminated Sources

A luminous source emits its own light; an illuminated source is seen because light reflects from it.

What's the difference between sunlight and moonlight? Sunlight is much brighter, sure. But more importantly, the Sun makes its own light, while the Moon only shines because it reflects sunlight. Everything you see fits one of these two groups. Objects like the Sun and other stars that emit their own light are luminous sources. Objects we see because light reflects off them, like the Moon and planets, are illuminated sources.

Luminous sources include flames, fireflies, TV screens, computer monitors, lasers, and tiny light-emitting diodes. In Figure 3, the fluorescent bulbs are the luminous source, turning electrical energy into light. Everything else in the room is illuminated by light reflecting off it. With no luminous source at all, you'd see nothing, because no light would reflect into your eyes.

5.title: Light and Matter
5.text:
Light and Matter

Opaque objects block light, translucent mediums transmit light without a clear view, and transparent mediums transmit most of the light that reaches them.

Objects can absorb, reflect, or transmit light. Objects that reflect and absorb light but don't transmit it are opaque, like books, people, and backpacks. Mediums that transmit and reflect light but don't let you see objects clearly through them are translucent, like the frosted glass in Figure 4. A transparent medium, like air or glass, transmits most of the light that reaches it.

Transparent mediums still reflect a little light. That's why you can see the clear candle holder itself! All three types absorb some light too, and opaque objects usually absorb the most.

So why can you see a fish through a glass fishbowl and also see the glass? The glass transmits most of the light, so light from the fish reaches you. It also reflects a little light, and that reflected light lets you see the bowl itself.

6.title: Luminous Flux
6.text:
Luminous Flux

Luminous flux is the rate at which a luminous source produces light energy, measured in lumens.

Imagine a flashlight shining at you from across the room. What decides how bright it looks? Three main things: how much light the flashlight produces, how far it is from your eye, and the angle at which the rays hit your eye. We'll explore the first two.

In the ray model, a brighter source sends out more rays. To capture all the light from a bulb, you'd have to surround it completely with a surface, as in Figure 5. The rate at which a luminous source produces light energy is its luminous flux, P, measured in lumens. The total light hitting that enclosing surface each second depends only on the source's luminous flux.

7.title: Illuminance
7.text:
Illuminance

Illuminance is the luminous flux falling on a given surface area, measured in lux, or lumens per square meter.

Once you know how much light a source emits, you can find how much lights up an object, like a book. The luminous flux falling on a surface area at any instant is the illuminance, E. It's measured in lux, which equals lumens per square meter. To keep things simple, we'll treat all light sources as point sources.

Look at Figure 6. The bulb's luminous flux is 1750 lumens, typical of a 26-watt compact fluorescent bulb. What's the illuminance on the inside of a sphere with a radius of 1.00 meter? All the flux lands on the sphere, so divide it by the sphere's area, 4 pi r squared. The area is 4 pi times the square of 1.00 meter, or 4 pi square meters. So the illuminance is 1750 lumens divided by 4 pi square meters, or 139 lux. That means 139 lumens strike each square meter.

testIt.name: Lumens
testIt.how: Change the bulb's lumens and read the lux on a 1.0 m sphere.

8.title: The Inverse-Square Relationship
8.text:
The Inverse-Square Relationship

The illuminance from a point source is proportional to one over the square of the distance from the source.

What if the sphere were bigger? With a radius of 2.00 meters, the flux is still 1750 lumens, because that depends only on the bulb. But the area is 4 pi times the square of 2.00 meters, or 16.0 pi square meters, four times bigger. So the illuminance is 1750 lumens over 16.0 pi square meters, or 34.8 lux. That's one-fourth as much.

With a 3.00-meter radius, the illuminance is only one-ninth as large, just 15.5 lumens per square meter. As rays spread out in straight lines from a point source, the number hitting each unit of area drops with the square of the distance. That's an inverse-square relationship.

Here's the math view. In E equals P over 4 pi r squared, if r stays the same, E is directly proportional to P: more flux, more illuminance. If P stays the same, E is inversely proportional to the square of r: as r increases, E decreases, and as r decreases, E increases.

testIt.name: Inverse square
testIt.how: Drag the sphere radius from 1 to 3 m for a 1000 lm bulb.

9.title: Luminous Intensity
9.text:
Luminous Intensity

Luminous intensity, measured in candelas, is the luminous flux that falls on 1 square meter of the inside of a sphere with a radius of 1 meter.

Some sources are rated in candelas. A candela isn't luminous flux but luminous intensity. For a point source, it's the flux falling on 1 square meter of the inside of a 1-meter sphere, so luminous intensity equals luminous flux divided by 4 pi. A 1750-lumen bulb has an intensity of 1750 divided by 4 pi, or 139 candelas.

In Figure 7, the lightbulb is twice as far from the screen as the candle. To light its side of the screen as brightly as the candle lights its side, the bulb needs four times the luminous intensity. If they had equal intensity, the bulb at twice the distance would give only one-quarter the illuminance. That's the inverse-square relationship again! So luminous intensity measures how strong the source is, and illuminance is what that source delivers to a surface at a given distance.

testIt.name: Photometer
testIt.how: Move the screen between a 64 cd bulb and a 1 cd candle 1.8 m apart until both sides match.

10.title: Point-Source Illuminance
10.text:
Point-Source Illuminance

The illuminance from a point source equals its luminous flux divided by 4 pi times the square of the distance.

Back to that flashlight. To make it look brighter, use a brighter bulb with more luminous flux, or move closer. For a point source, the illuminance follows this equation: E equals P divided by 4 pi times the square of r. Only a fraction of the flux reaches the object, because the light spreads in all directions.

The equation works only when light hits the surface straight on, at a right angle, and when the source is small enough or far enough away to count as a point. So it isn't accurate for long fluorescent tubes or for bulbs very close to a surface.

Architects lighting a classroom must think about the lights' luminous flux, how high they hang above the desks, and how efficient they are, which affects cost. For even lighting, engineers usually space lights evenly, like in your classroom. They also design special lights that control how the beam spreads. That's vital for car headlights, as in Figure 8, because headlights set at the wrong angle leave dark patches on the road.

11.title: Example Problem 1, Illumination of a Surface
11.text:
Example Problem 1, Illumination of a Surface

E equals P over 4 pi r squared applies when light strikes a surface perpendicularly.

What's the illuminance on your desk if it's lit by a 1750-lumen lamp 2.50 meters above it?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Treat the bulb as a point source. Sketch the bulb above the desk and label P and r. Known: P equals 1.75 times ten to the third lumens, and r equals 2.50 meters. Unknown: E.

Step two: solve. The light hits the desk straight on, so use the point-source equation. E equals P over 4 pi times the square of r. Substitute 1.75 times ten to the third lumens over 4 pi times the square of 2.50 meters. That's 22.3 lumens per square meter, or 22.3 lux.

Step three: evaluate. Lumens per square meter is lux, so the units are right. All quantities are positive, as they should be. And is it realistic? A 1750-lumen lamp at 1.00 meter gives 139 lux, so at 2.50 meters, more than twice as far, the illuminance should be less than one-fourth of that. 22.3 lux fits!

testIt.name: Desk lamp
testIt.how: Raise or lower the 1750 lm lamp above your desk.

12.title: The Speed of Light and Clues from Io
12.text:
The Speed of Light and Clues from Io

Ole Roemer was the first to successfully measure how long light takes to travel between two points.

People have argued that light travels at a finite speed for more than 2400 years. By the seventeenth century, experiments suggested it was finite but much faster than sound. Measuring it was tough, though. Light crosses distances on Earth far faster than human reaction time!

Danish astronomer Ole Roemer found a way. Between 1668 and 1674, he made 70 measurements of the 1.8-day orbit of Io, one of Jupiter's moons, timing when Io came out of Jupiter's shadow, as in Figure 10. He was helping improve maps by figuring out longitude, an early case of technology driving science.

Roemer could predict the next eclipse, but the actual times didn't match. Io's period seemed about 13 seconds longer per orbit when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and about 13 seconds shorter when Earth was approaching. Roemer figured Jupiter's moons were as regular as our Moon, so he looked at another variable: Earth's own motion and position relative to Jupiter.

testIt.how: Move Earth around its orbit and see how late Io's eclipse looks.

13.title: Measuring the Speed of Light
13.text:
Measuring the Speed of Light

The speed of light in a vacuum, c, is defined as 299,792,458 meters per second.

Roemer reasoned that as Earth moved away from Jupiter, light from each eclipse had farther to go, so it arrived later. In the 182.5 days Earth took to go from position 1 to position 3, there were 182.5 days divided by 1.8 days per eclipse, about 1.0 times ten to the second eclipses. At 13 seconds each, that's 1.3 times ten to the third seconds, about 22 minutes, for light to cross Earth's orbit. Using today's value for the orbit's diameter, about 2.99 times ten to the eleventh meters, his 22 minutes gives a speed of about 2.3 times ten to the eighth meters per second. Today we know light takes about 16.6 minutes, not 22. Still, Roemer proved light has a finite speed!

The most famous measurements came from American physicist Albert A. Michelson, who refined Earth-based methods from 1880 into the 1920s. In 1926, he timed light's round trip between two California mountains 35 kilometers apart. His best result was 2.99796 times ten to the eighth meters per second, plus or minus 0.00004 times ten to the eighth. He was the first American to win a Nobel Prize in science, honored for his precision optical instruments and measurements.

The speed of light in a vacuum gets the symbol c, defined as exactly 299,792,458 meters per second. For most problems, 3.00 times ten to the eighth meters per second works fine. At that speed, light travels 9.46 times ten to the twelfth kilometers in a year. That distance is a light-year.

So, how does distance affect how bright a star appears? A star is a luminous point source sending its light out in all directions. Twice as far away, the same light spreads over four times the area, so it looks one-fourth as bright. The illuminance falls with the square of the distance.

testIt.how: Set a star's distance and watch its brightness fall.
